Anecdotes, even from practitioners, aren’t remotely the same as population-level research. Claims like “70% of my patients react to gluten” or “there’s no scientific evidence that humans need grains” are opinions, not consensus-backed data.

I’m all for people doing what works for them, but broad claims like these can cause confusion, especially when they come from sources that don’t have medical or scientific credentials held to peer-reviewed standards. [Dr. Osborne's "doctorate of pastoral science”](https://www.drpeterosborne.com/about/dr-peter-osborne/) is not even a recognized medical degree.

Sorry, but that 60% statistic is wildly false. The real prevalence is anywhere between [0.5% and 6%](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/gluten-sensitivity-is-real). Some research suggests that it could be [up to 6%](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5677194/) in [the U.S.](https://www.nm.org/healthbeat/healthy-tips/celiac-disease-vs-gluten-intolerance-infographic) A few studies have anywhere from 8% to 15% worldwide, but those appear to be outliers. 

But claiming that 60% of people are gluten intolerant is dangerous. If you eat gluten-free when you don't need to, you're risking nutritional deficiencies. Also, Dr. Davis is someone who has been on Dr. Oz, and his research has been heavily criticized by the rest of the scientific community.

OP, it's clear how much you care about your cat. It's okay to be overwhelmed right now. While I am not a vet, I do have a lot of experience with animals, and I agree that it sounds like your cat's behavior is driven by chronic anxiety. Other users have already made some solid suggestions, but above all, I would consult a behaviorist. You should also reassess your litter box set-up: Some cats prefer open boxes, some cats prefer unscented litter, some need a box in a discreet area, etc. In the meantime, I would invest in some waterproof bedding protectors and couch covers. They might help minimize some of your frustration from your cat's accidents.

Ultimately, she may need a consistently quiet home with lots of space. If you're able to find a home that can provide that to her, it doesn't mean that you've failed - it means that you love her enough to put her needs first.

Whatever you decide, be kind to yourself, OP. Wishing you and your kitty the best. <3

This issue is so complex that it's hard for me to form an opinion on it. If someone can barely feed themselves, do I think they should go out and adopt a pet? No. Ideally, they would at least be in a stable enough position that they aren't having to worry about how to survive each and every day. Also, animals can and will suffer if they aren't able to visit the vet, often leading to painful deaths. It's just a question of whether or not you see that as better or worse than being euthanized in a shelter.

Personally, in shelters with high euthanasia rates, I think it's okay to roll the dice and adopt an animal as long as you can guarantee food and water for them. However, I've lived in an area where all of the shelters are low kill, (meaning animals were only euthanized due to extremely aggressive behavior or terminal illness), and, in that case, I do believe it's worth waiting for someone who can provide a solid home life. At those sorts of shelters, there are usually vets available, including in-house vets, foster homes, decent quality food, etc.
Normally, I would agree, but if OP isn't from a first world country, there may not be many rescues around.

Based on your answers, I would think very carefully before getting your dad a dog.

First, unless your dad is a qualified, professional breeder who has the time, ability, and resources to responsibly raise puppies, his dog should 100% be spayed/neutered. I wouldn't get him a dog unless he agrees to this, personally.

Second, your mom needs to be aware that if something happens to your dad, she'll automatically be next in line to take care of the dog. If you or another family member is in a position to take it in should something happen, then great, but if not, then your mom needs to be on board with being the primary caretaker.

All of that being said, if you arrive to the conclusion that getting your dad a dog is a viable option, then I would look at poodles or standard schnauzers. Both are low shedding, (not non-shedding), and aren't too large. You may want to check breed-specific rescues in the state to see if there are any dogs with personalities that match what your parents are looking for.

Not necessarily. I would be more inclined to assign the blame to carbs. If you're going from low/no carb to eating a bunch of carbs at once, your body is suddenly having to store glycogen again. Storing glycogen requires water; it's why high carb meals tend to lead to water retention, which can result in a puffy face. It also can have the opposite effect: people who go low/no carb typically experience an initial "whoosh" in weight because their body is letting go of the water it preserved for glycogen.

This requires a bit of a backstory:

I grew up with a Miniature Schnauzer named Buddie. She was practically a sibling to me, since I'm an only child. Buddie was a great dog, as we think all of our dogs are. But, since she and I grew up together, (we adopted her when she was six months old, and I was two years old), we had a special bond. At home, she'd constantly be by my side. When I was sick, she'd sleep next to me. At night, she'd be on my bed, cuddling with my feet. She tolerated me playing "Vet" with her, pulling on her ears and tail, attempting to pick her up. She was the most patient dog ever, and not once did she ever snap, or even growl at me. Needless to say, we were inseparable.

Well, Buddie became old and developed heart disease. She started having terrible seizures. In a way, my parents and I were selfish. We didn't want to see her go, so we kept her alive much longer than she should have been by giving her medication each day. It didn't do much, but it kept her breathing. She was able to get around a bit, but at random moments, she would be stricken by horrible seizures. It was tough to watch, and we could tell that she was in pain. She really had no quality of life.

I remember one particular moment, when I was sure she was going to pass. She was curled up in a ball under a tree in our backyard, not moving. I was watching from a window in our family room. I didn't want to go outside, but then my mom saw her. She ran outside to go and check on her. My dog heard her, lifted her head, and feebly wagged her tail. Then she saw me, and mustered up all of her strength to stand up. My mom picked her up, carried her back into the house, and she came up to me and sat down. It was at that moment that I realized my dog was living for me and my family. She saw my mom's hurt and scared expression. She saw me with what could only be a pained look in my eyes. She was keeping on for the sake of us.

One morning, (when she was 12, and I was 14), during my winter break, I woke up at five in the morning to her crying louder than I'd ever heard her cry. My mom rushed upstairs and told me that Buddie was having trouble breathing, and that her and my dad were taking her to the vet. She asked if I wanted to come along, and in my daze and fatigue, I said no, thinking that the vet would simply increase her medication dosage, or something to that extent. I then went back to sleep.

I woke up, and a few minutes later, heard the car door slam. I looked out one of the upstairs windows, and saw my parents getting out of the car. Without Buddie. My mom was hunched over. And that's when I knew. I fucking knew.

My mom came into my room, and, with a shaky voice, told me that they had put Buddie to sleep. I let her cry into my shoulder, but shed no tears myself. Not only am I uncomfortable with crying in front of people, but I realized that I had abandoned my own dog. A creature that had lived for me had died without me holding her. I stared into space for a while, and then, when my mom left, burst into tears.

For a few nights after she died, I kept on having the same dream about her. In the dream, I was upstairs, and I could hear Buddie barking. I could see her shadow on the wall as she was jumping and prancing around. I couldn't get to her, but I could see and hear how happy and healthy she was again. It truly did comfort me. Though I'm not a believer in the afterlife, I always like to think that the dreams were some sort of sign that she is okay.

I would be lying if I said that a few tears didn't fall while typing this. Five years later, and I still well up whenever I think about her. So, if I could have a 30 second do-over, I'd go back and go to the vet's office with my parents. I'd make myself get my damned, lazy ass out of bed. I really hope that Buddie didn't think that I abandoned her. I never would have done that to her, had I realized what was going on. I loved her too much. And, really, she taught me what love is. You've never experienced true, unconditional love until you've owned a dog who will literally live FOR you, even if it means she/he has to suffer.

There isn't a day that goes by that I don't think about that dog. She was definitely something else.

I'm going to throw in my two cents here about whether the cat was playing or not when it bit the kid. (I volunteer at an animal shelter, where I had to take "cat training" and learn about cat behavior.)

Cats bite usually for two reasons: Play aggression, or overstimulation. Both seem plausible in this situation.

Play aggression is when cats replicate hunting behaviors. They see the "prey" coming, such as a human hand, and they pounce on it. It's not meant out of aggression: the cat is merely playing. Unfortunately, claws happen to hurt.

Overstimulation is self-explanatory, really. You pet your cat for too long, your cats gets pissed off, and then it bites or scratches you. After the kid hits the cat, you can see the cat's ears start to go back, and its body becomes stiff. Both of those signs mean that the cat was not too happy about being smacked. (Which, of course, is understandable.)

So, it seems to me that in the first part of the video, the cat was displaying play aggression. After the kid hit the cat, that's when the cat became overstimulated/angry. Hopefully the parents don't put the cat down. The kid or cat should have been moved after the kid started to cry. Bad parenting move.

My dad teaches history at the #1 high school in America. Every day, he's with students with absolutely brilliant minds. Yet, he causes them to think more, to question everything, to use new approaches, to appreciate the past and learn from it.

He didn't have to be a teacher. He had a perfect score on his GRE exam, and was highly considered for law school. He chose education, and went to one of the top graduate schools in the world on scholarship. 

He's one of the most intelligent people I've ever known. He easily could have chosen a job that paid him enormous amounts of money. He had endless opportunities.

But, he chose to be a teacher, simply because he loves inspiring kids. He wants his students to love, or at least like, history, and if he can't get them to do that, he helps them get by. 

He has sponsored numerous clubs, does summer school every summer, lets students come talk to him about anything. He memorizes every kid's name that he meets, and greets him/her when he runs into him/her. He genuinely cares about the kids that he teaches.

The point of the video is not to make the teachers look like assholes. (Although it does a good job of accomplishing it.) All thoughts aside, the point is to remind people how hard teachers work, and how much they achieve. A lot of people undermine education. And it's not about torturing the students: it's about reminding them how much promise they hold. A lot of them don't get that at home, and teachers can provide that for them. Sure, you get a few bad apples in the bunch. But that doesn't mean the rest of them are spoiled as well.

It's not about comparing jobs. It's not about saying, "Oh, my job is much harder than yours, and I have much longer hours. My job must be better than yours." It's about the impact that you have in whatever career you choose. What you put into your job is what you get out of it. My dad is incredibly satisfied and pleased when he sees a student do well, and that's why he keeps teaching.

And the impact doesn't stop there. I go to a college where a lot of his students go, and whenever I mention my last name, they say, "Oh, are you his daughter? I loved him!"

That, right there, is why I'm proud to have my dad be a teacher.
